head.function: Your brain is the control center of your body. It controls thoughts, memory, speech and movement. Good sleep helps you think clearly, react quickly and keep a steady mood.
head.spaceflight: Astronauts see 16 sunrises and sunsets a day on the station, which can disrupt sleep. Isolation and confinement may affect sleep, morale and decision making.

eyes.function: Cells in the retina turn light into electrical signals. These signals travel through the optic nerve to the brain.
eyes.spaceflight: Weightlessness shifts body fluids toward the head. This can swell the optic nerve and fold the retina, a set of eye and brain changes called SANS.

heart.function: The heart pumps blood through your body. Arteries, veins and capillaries carry the oxygen and nutrients your organs need.
heart.spaceflight: Low gravity can change the heart and blood vessels, even making the heart more spherical. After landing, low blood pressure can make fainting more likely.

skeleton.function: Your bones help you move, give you shape and support your body. Your muscles help you move and help your body work.
skeleton.spaceflight: On 4-6 month missions, bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their density each month, so daily exercise protects bone and muscle.

body.function: Your immune system defends the body against infections and other diseases. Normal body temperature varies with age, activity and time of day; over 100.4°F (38°C) usually means a fever.
body.spaceflight: Radiation, microgravity and poor sleep can change the immune system. Astronauts get more radiation in space than on Earth, which can raise cancer risk.

gut.function: Your digestive system breaks food down so your body can use it for energy and to build cells. It absorbs nutrients and water, and gut bacteria help with digestion.
gut.spaceflight: Keeping astronauts healthy in space requires adequate nutrition. The microbes in astronauts' guts change during spaceflight.
